To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) metal contamination by dry fallout of atmospheric deposition was less than one percent of the metal contamination of plant leaves; (ii) the main pathway of Hg contamination was foliar absorption; (iii) the main pathway for Cu contamination was root absorption; (iv) the main pathway to Zn contamination was root absorption and (v) metal solubility in sediment was increased by the vegetal cover.

1) Hg is the metal of concern in dredged sediment; 2) metal solubility in sediment is enhanced when vegetal cover is established; 3) Hg contamination in vegetal cover may be enhanced by the establishment of vegeta cover; 4) the use of grasses in phytostablisation may enhance the metal solubility of contaminated sediment.
the metal availability in a contaminated dredged sediment was increased in the presence of a vegetal cover, especially when the vegetal cover was a rape crop.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fate of metals and Hg in the soil plant system and the impact of a vegetal cover.
the potential of grass cover plants to increase the solubility of metals in dredged sediment.
a new approach for the assessment of the potential risks of contaminated dredged sediment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the establishment of a vegetal cover on a metal-contaminated dredged sediment may increase metal availability in ground waters and also the metal transfer to plants.

the vegetal cover of dredged sediment with grass is a good solution for phytostabilising the metal contamination of the sediment, but it is not sufficient for reducing Hg contamination of the sediment.
metal transfer from contaminated dredged sediment to plant is possible but is dependent on the metal and plant species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the establishment of grass cover in phytostablisation may be beneficial for Cu, but not for Zn.
the establishment of vegetative cover on a dredged sediment may increase metal availability for the plants.
the establishment of a vegetal cover on dredged sediments could induce an increase of metal solublisation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Hg transfer to plant leaves by dry deposition is low and that foliar absorption of volatile mercury is the major pathway for HG transfer.
the use of a vegetal cover in phytostabilsation of dredged sedments contaminated with metals may increase metal solubility and the transfer of metals to plants.
the vegetal cover of contaminated sediments may increase the metal solubility and consequently the metal bioavailability.
